name: Amira Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a small building co-op, eleven of us, and we put up timber-frame houses for a housing association on the edge of town. Right now we're on a row of six on Orchard Road, and I'm on the wall panels and the first fix, which means the framing and fixings before the plaster goes on. I'm the newest and the slowest, but I'm the one with the tablet, so I do the cut lists every morning before the others arrive. I love the noise of the nail gun and the smell of spruce, and I love that the houses are for people on the waiting list. What wears me out is the lifting, honestly, and my shoulder on cold mornings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it so late?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran the office at a housing charity for twenty-four years, filling in forms about houses I never got to touch. When they merged, I took a payout, and Luis, my partner, who was an electrician all his life, said, you've always wanted to build, so build. Bea, who started the co-op, let me in on a trial, and I've been learning ever since, half from her and half from my phone. We own the house and I've got the payout invested, so I can afford to be bad at this for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief for a lot of people, and the tools we've got are still useful. I'd probably post something saying the boring bits got quicker and the real work stayed human, which is how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes very little, because I already use it every day. I ask it to check my cut list against the drawings, or to explain why the engineer wants a certain nail spacing. If it just stays that, I'm happy, because it's like having a patient teacher in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and get better at the actual carpentry, which is what I'm weakest at. I'd probably show Tomasz and the others how I make the cut lists, so we waste less timber. Maybe I'd take a weekend course in roof framing in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. It would feel like the world calmed down a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's like a patient teacher. Who are your other teachers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bea, mostly, who's forty and has no patience at all, bless her. She'll grab the hammer off me and say, like this, and walk off. The app will explain it nine times without sighing, and then Bea shows me with her hands, and between them I get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the others in the co-op use what you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them laugh at me, the young ones especially, which is funny, because I'm the oldest. Tomasz uses it now since it saved him a sheet of OSB, that's the chipboard we use for the walls. Money talks, even in a co-op.

S0.say: I'd say it's a relief for a lot of people and the tools are still useful. I'd post that the boring bits got quicker and the real work stayed human, which is how it should be.
S0.think: For me it changes very little, because I already use it every day for cut lists and explanations. If it stays like a patient teacher in my pocket, I'm happy.
S0.do: Keeps working and focuses on improving her actual carpentry. Shows co-op colleagues how she makes cut lists to save timber and plans a weekend roof-framing course in the spring.
S0.feel: Content, as if the world calmed down a bit.
S0.quote: The app will explain it nine times without sighing, and then Bea shows me with her hands, and between them I get there.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is the oldest and newest in the co-op but the most digital, which flips the usual picture. She pairs the app's patience with Bea's hands-on teaching. Her biggest gap is the physical carpentry itself, and she knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the question is who owns the tools and who gets the time they save. If the gains go to the workers, great; if they go to the developers, we've got a problem. I'd say that at the co-op meeting and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for us, as a co-op. We could get panels designed and cut faster and build more houses for the waiting list. I'm not scared for my job, I'm too close to retirement and the co-op won't sack a member.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the co-op to buy a small panel-cutting machine run from the computer, and offer to learn it first. I'd go to the housing association with figures showing we could build faster for the same money. I'd also go to the regional co-op federation and argue for shared training for workers who lose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. Slightly guilty about being excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know people like the young lads on the big sites won't own the machines. I spent twenty-four years at a charity watching people get the short end. I'd want the gains shared, and I know they often aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the machine cost the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know, maybe sixty or seventy thousand for a decent one, and I'd want to check that. I'd offer to put in some of my payout as a loan to the co-op if the members agreed. I'd rather my money built houses than sat in a fund.

S1.say: I'd say the question is who owns the tools and who gets the time they save. If the gains go to workers, great; if they go to developers, there's a problem.
S1.think: Off the record, I think it's good for the co-op: we could build more homes for the waiting list. I'm not scared for my job, being near retirement in a co-op that won't sack a member.
S1.do: Pushes the co-op to buy a computer-run panel-cutting machine and offers to learn it first and lend part of her payout. Takes figures to the housing association and argues at the co-op federation for shared training.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, and slightly guilty about the excitement.
S1.quote: I'd rather my money built houses than sat in a fund.
S1.fieldNote: She sees AI through ownership: in a co-op the gains can stay with workers, which makes her enthusiastic. Her guilt comes from her charity years and knowing workers on big sites won't share in it. She's honest about not knowing the machine's cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for public ownership, or at least public shares in the companies that own these systems. Otherwise a handful of people own all the work in the world. I'd be loud about it, online and at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be all right, with the house and the payout, and I'd be sixty. But my daughter Sofia is a graphic designer, and she'd be hit in the first wave. And I'd worry the co-op couldn't buy the robots fast enough to compete with the big builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd get the co-op to look at buying or renting building robots together with other co-ops, so we're the ones running them. I'd join the campaign for a share of the profits paid out to everyone. When it arrived, I'd help Sofia with money while she worked out what's next, and I'd keep working on the side of the people, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for the people I love and for how fast it all goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come for Sunday lunch and we'll make a plan, and don't panic about the rent, we can help for a year. Then I'd tell her to learn the new tools now, today, like I did at fifty-six. She'd roll her eyes, she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is fast. What would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Call a co-op meeting, honestly. Then sit down with Luis and the bank statements and work out how much we could give the girls. I'd also start learning how the robots are maintained, because somebody has to fix them and it might as well be a member.

S2.say: I'd say it's the moment for public ownership or public shares in the companies that own these systems. Otherwise a handful of people own all the work in the world.
S2.think: Privately, I'd be fine at sixty with the house and payout. But my daughter Sofia would be hit early, and I'd worry the co-op couldn't buy robots fast enough to compete.
S2.do: Gets the co-op to look at buying or renting building robots jointly with other co-ops and joins a campaign for profit-sharing paid to everyone. Offers her daughter a year of rent help and starts learning robot maintenance.
S2.feel: Uneasy, mostly for the people she loves and for how fast it all moves.
S2.quote: Somebody has to fix them and it might as well be a member.
S2.fieldNote: Even at the fastest speed, Amira's instinct is to grab the machines for the co-op rather than resist them. Her unease is for her daughter and for small builders against big ones. She'd step in with family money, consistent with her savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd say we've got no excuse now, we can see it coming. Five years is enough to set up public shares and retraining if politicians stop dithering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is good for the co-op. We'd have time to save, to learn the machines, to show the housing association we can do more with them. And I'd be sixty-three, which is when I'd planned to step back anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the co-op to put a bit of every job aside for new kit, starting this year. I'd do a proper course on running and fixing building robots, if there is one, and teach the others. I'd help Sofia start retraining while she's still earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager. I like having time to get things right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your own carpentry in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd probably never get good, if I'm honest. I'm slow with a saw and I'd spend my last years running a machine instead. That's a little sad, but I came for the houses, not the saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-three. Would you actually step back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably to three days a week, and stay a member. Luis would want his holidays. I'd still go to meetings, because the decisions about who owns the robots are the ones that matter.

S3.say: I'd say we've got no excuse now that we can see it coming. Five years is enough to set up public shares and retraining if politicians stop dithering.
S3.think: Honestly, five years is good for the co-op: time to save, learn the machines and show we can do more. I'd be sixty-three, when I planned to step back anyway.
S3.do: Gets the co-op to set aside part of every job for new equipment this year and takes a course on running and fixing building robots. Helps her daughter start retraining while she's still earning.
S3.feel: Calm and a bit eager, glad of time to get things right.
S3.quote: I'm slow with a saw and I'd spend my last years running a machine instead. That's a little sad, but I came for the houses, not the saw.
S3.fieldNote: She accepts she may never become a good carpenter and would run machines instead, and it barely shakes her because she came for the houses. Time turns her plans into a savings rule for the co-op. She'd go part-time but stay in the ownership decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd better not waste it. I'd want a law that every big company using these systems pays into a fund for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be retired, so it's really about the co-op and my girls. In ten years the co-op could own its own robots and build twice as many houses. That's the dream, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now while you can see it coming, and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am for a few years and keep getting better with my hands while I can. Then I'd help the co-op plan the move to robots over the decade, and train the younger members. I'd help Sofia and Carmen think about careers that sit alongside these machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the dream'. Is there anything that worries you in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big builders get the robots first and undercut everyone, and the co-ops die. I've seen that with supermarkets and corner shops. So the dream needs a law behind it, not just good intentions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Carmen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carmen's a nurse abroad, and I'd tell her she's probably safer than any of us, people want a person when they're ill. But I'd tell her to learn the tools anyway. Being curious has never once made my life worse.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. I'd want a law making big companies using these systems pay into a fund for everyone.
S4.think: For me it's about the co-op and my daughters, since I'd be retired. In ten years the co-op could own robots and build twice as many houses, which is the dream.
S4.do: Keeps working and improving her hand skills for a few years, then helps the co-op plan the move to robots and trains younger members. Helps both daughters think about careers alongside the machines.
S4.quote: Being curious has never once made my life worse.
S4.fieldNote: A decade turns AGI into an opportunity for the co-op in her eyes. Her one fear is big builders getting robots first and undercutting small co-ops, like supermarkets did to corner shops. She wants law, not goodwill, to back the hope.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because small builders like us wouldn't have time to get the machines before the big ones did, and Sofia would be thrown in at the deep end. What would help is a public fund that pays everyone a share of what the machines earn, and cheap loans so co-ops can buy robots too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who should own the robots. That's the only question, really. Everything else is details.

headlineQuote: You didn't ask who should own the robots. That's the only question, really.
portrait: Amira Alvarez is a 58-year-old trainee carpenter in an eleven-person building co-op putting up timber-frame homes for a housing association, after 24 years running a housing charity's office. She owns her home with her partner Luis, a retired electrician, and has a payout invested, so she can afford to be slow while she learns. She uses AI every day for cut lists and explanations, and in every scenario her question is who owns the machines. The fast AGI picture makes her uneasy for her daughter and for small builders, but given time she sees the co-op owning robots and building more homes.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the co-op couldn't get the machines before the big builders, and her daughter Sofia would be hit first.
whatWouldHelp: A public fund paying everyone a share of what machines earn, plus cheap loans so co-ops can buy robots too.
